utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Good morning to you. Could you be kind enough to call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Andrew Cayley assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager, good morning Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman and I'm with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. So good morning, everybody. You know that this is a Status Conference that the Chamber had decided to hold, specifying also the date, and this was before Mr. Ackerman himself included an ad hoc request for holding of a Status Conference in one of his last -- one of his motions. I suppose we need to go through all this one point after another. I have my agenda which I have prepared, which, however, seems to have disappeared. But basically -- oh, here it is. The reason for this Status Conference is more or less something that has already been stated, made clear, during the last sitting or two sittings. This is a consequence mainly of the severance of the two accused, of the two trials, and also as I understood it when we first started discussing the possibility of a Status Conference, also the need which was felt at a time to have some amendments made to the indictment, as well as the reorganisation of the case for the Prosecution, which to me seemed to be something which was obvious that needed to be done. Since we last met, we have had some developments. There was one motion from General Talic to revoke the order for severance and also accompanying it, in the sense that it's related to it, another motion which asked for staying of proceedings and also time to file written submissions, further written submissions on it. That matter has been decided. The first of these motions was actually a request was for certification. That was served -- the English version was served on you, Mr. Ackerman, as lead counsel and the matter was decided last Thursday or Friday. Certification being denied. After that, the second of the -- the second motion was also decided in the same decision, which was to give time for the filing of submissions and in the meantime to stay proceedings. That was also rejected. And following the filing of the decision of this Trial Chamber rejecting certification, requested certification, the Trial Chamber received an another motion from General Talic which we don't need to discuss here because basically now it belongs to that trial and not this one, and whether it will be decided or whether it needs to be decided or not is a matter that does not concern you. But I'm just briefing you to put you in the complete picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just before you leave that, we haven't filed a response to that because again we didn't know whether -- which Trial Chamber or whatever is seized of it. But in any event, Your Honour, we took the view that it was otiose, we didn't require to file a response to it, because in fact, you had already made a decision on the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But if Your Honours or whichever Trial Chamber deals with that matter requires a response, then perhaps your clerk would let it be good enough to let us know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically, the way we looked at the matter, you know I mean that as experienced lawyers and we as experienced judges know that when something like this happens, sometimes you get a motion and you don't know exactly in which compartment to put it, or from which house to -- which bakery to bake it. And the decision that we took since it was a request for certification leading to possibly revocation, we decided that it belonged to the joint trial at the time and not to Talic's trial separately. So what happens to the last motion, I tell you, I will involve Mr. Ackerman as Defence counsel for Mr. Brdjanin if it's the case of involving him. You definitely will need to be involved because whichever compartment that needs to be put in, you're always the Prosecutor in this case. As far as the rest is concerned, we have point number 1 that I would like to deal with, and I think it can be dealt with very easily, at the time this Chamber had -- was still considering Talic's request for certification and the accompanying motion, you, Mr. Ackerman, filed a -- another motion of your own, asking for a delay in hearing witness or proceeding with the case until the matter of the certification was decided. Now, we have decided that issue and so am I right in taking it that that motion is now to be considered moot?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's point number 1 that is being made. That's for the Registrar and also my staff, Mr. Brdjanin's motion of last week asking for a delay in the continuation of the proceedings pending the decision on the certification is now moot. Then we had concurrently two sets of documents coming from both sides, which have a -- converge on something which is basic to the continuation of this trial. And that is following an indication which we had from the Prosecution during the last sitting, that was also as a consequence of a verbal remark that you made, Mr. Ackerman, an indication that the Prosecution will be seeking to amend to some extent the indictment. At the same time, you came forward with an ad hoc motion for the -- request for the amendment of the indictment and also for the proceedings not to go ahead before the indictment is actually and effectively amended. And I think that that is the next point that needs to be taken up in this Status Conference. May I just, in order to streamline and make everybody's task easier, remind you of what was stated way back --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start from the first of October. Basically on that day, Mr. Ackerman, you asked that a new indictment be filed and that the case be stayed until this new indictment was actually filed and accepted or endorsed by this Chamber as required by the rules. At the time, we invited you to make submissions on -- or rather you asked, Mr. Ackerman, that we invite the Prosecution and you to make submissions on which evidence tendered so far is relevant to Brdjanin's case and should be incorporated into the records of this case. As a result of these two specific requests, we agreed at the time that we would be convening this Status Conference. Two days later, that is on the 3rd of October, the Prosecution filed a response and specifically, this Chamber was asked to reject the request for the stay of proceedings, to the -- deny, reject, the request, the parties make submissions regarding the relevance of evidence which had already been admitted in the trial, and to order that the proposed amended indictment that was filed on the same day be approved for the duration of the trial against your client, Brdjanin. The Prosecution on the same day requested leave to amend the indictment as per the document which has been circulated. There are two documents relating to possible amendments to the indictment. Some amendments that have been suggested by the Defence for Brdjanin have been incorporated in the proposed amendments by the Prosecution. Some others do not feature in the proposed amendments. So I would suggest first and foremost to ask the Prosecution to elaborate on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Elaborate on what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: About -- there are some further proposed amendments to the indictment forthcoming from the Defence -- from the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which have not been incorporated. I don't know whether at the time you drafted and filed the proposed amendments you also had all the amendments that were in front of you, all of the amendments that were being proposed by the Defence because it may well be that there are some amendments that you don't have any difficulty in incorporating now with hindsight or it may well be completely different from what I'm suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have amended the indictment in the way we think is the correct way. May I say we didn't go through all of Mr. Ackerman's objections or changes. We looked at the indictment and worked out what was the correct way to produce a severed version of it and those are the amendments we seek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, do you have any comments on it this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I received the proposed amended indictment 20 or 30 minutes ago and I haven't had a chance to even go through it at all. That's the first I've seen it. It was in my box when I arrived here this morning. It was not faxed to me in Texas. It was not at my office here when I arrived here, so I have just had the first opportunity to look at it. I've looked at it for maybe five minutes but certainly, not any opportunity to look at it in depth at all. I don't know where to go from this point other than it's very difficult for me to make any kind after response regarding that indictment until I've had several hours at least to go through it and compare it and think about it. And I'm sorry about that but it's nothing that I could avoid in any way. I didn't know there had been an amended indictment filed until I arrived here this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, there will not be several hours. We will go through it bit by bit. Take your indictments out, please. The Prosecutor's corrected version of the fourth amended indictment of the 10th December, 2001. We go to para 10 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it helps Mr. Ackerman what we've done, in essence, is remove any charging language as against Talic in the indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that's enough for Mr. Ackerman, because I have -- I didn't have it faxed but I had all the documentation with me and I spent a whole weekend going through paragraph by paragraph -- through it paragraph by paragraph, comparing the two texts in juxtaposition with what Mr. Ackerman was suggesting and there are several points. It won't take us a long time. Don't worry, it will take us much less time to go through this exercise than if I were to give the couple of hours to Mr. Ackerman that he has asked for. So para 10.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, the interpreters do not have a copy of that indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I need my copy. Do you have a copy of the ...? Yes, Inneke has one. Sorry, Inneke I'm going to deprive you of your copy. And if the Prosecution -- you have the proposed amended indictment, Mr. Ackerman, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So just open the two indictments, please. Para 10. The Defence for Talic -- for Brdjanin asks for the removal or the deletion in para 10 of any reference to Talic's membership in the ARK Crisis Staff. Essentially, what the Prosecution has done is not what Mr. Ackerman requested. It has only removed the bold characterisation of Momir Talic so that the text essentially remains the same except that Momir Talic in the amended, fourth amended indictment, appears in bold characters while in the proposed amended indictment, it is in normal characters. So here we have the first variation or difference. Mr. Ackerman, do you insist on --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the status of the situation as is exists today is this: The Prosecution has presented absolutely no evidence that General Talic ever attended any meeting of the ARK Crisis Staff or was ever actually a member of that staff other than one document upon which his name appears. If -- on para 10 of the indictment, it's the intention of the Prosecutor to set out who the members of the Crisis Staff were, then that's one thing. But to name only two, Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic seems to be leaving the indictment basically in the state of a joint indictment of Brdjanin and Talic. If it is the Prosecutor's intention with regard to para 10 to set out in that paragraph who the members of the Crisis Staff were, including General Talic, then that's the way it should be done but otherwise, it is not a Brdjanin-specific paragraph but it's a Brdjanin-Talic paragraph. That's my objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I reply, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour firstly, this is a -- if you like -- an abstract of the original joint indictment as it developed through the various orders that were made by Judge Hunt as to the detail that was to be provided. It would have course be possible to apply to amend to put in a number of other details but in our submission, they are necessary. Later on in the indictment, there is reference to other members of the ARK Crisis Staff. The fact is that at this stage, it is a matter for us subject to Your Honour's rulings, as to who we wish to name at this really background paragraph. As to evidence, there is clear, unambiguous evidence that General Talic was named --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Leave that because the purpose of this Status Conference is not to establish whether there is evidence or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very well, then Your Honour as far as we are concerned unless there is something wrong in law with that pleading, we submit that we are justified and indeed properly correct because effectively it's still, going right back, it's all one joint indictment against three men but each one has been amended through the process of these hearings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So para 10 -- para 12, sorry. The Defence for Brdjanin objects to the retention in the indictment any reference to Talic's presence on the 12th of May, 1992 meeting of the assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the decision to create the army of the VRS, Talic being amended commander of the 1st Krajina Corps of the VRS and the 1st Krajina Corps engaging in military operations in the municipalities included within the area of the ARK. Basically, this is what is being objected to. In reality, one sees the proposed amended indictment again we just have the whole paragraph retained as it is, with the exception of the name of Momir Talic no longer appearing in bold characters. Now, Mr. Ackerman, do you want to sustain your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think a lot of these paragraphs, the same argument applies. And it basically is that if you look at the original indictment in this case, against Mr. Brdjanin only, you don't see any of this language that went into the indictment after General Talic became a defendant in the case, and now, all the Prosecutor is doing is just removing the boldface type but leaving the indictment the same as a joint indictment against Brdjanin-Talic. There is another person involved in this indictment whose name has now been made public but you find his name no where in here, bold or otherwise. And the Prosecutor is really trying to simply conform this indictment to a Brdjanin-specific indictment just by taking out the bold type in General Talic's name but we are in a whole different universe here at this point. This used to be an indictment involving the military. It's no longer an indictment involving the military. Mr. Brdjanin is not military. And Mr. Brdjanin had nothing to do with the military, had no control whatsoever over the military, and to continue this indictment as if there is a military component to it I suggest to you is improper and it must be changed in many of the ways that I've suggested. And I think this argument will apply to a number of the paragraphs, Your Honour, so I won't have to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I make it clear and I think this will deal with it. First of all, Mr. Ackerman is wrong. The original indictment was against three persons, Brdjanin, Talic, and Zupljanin. It was always a joint indictment but because each person was separately arrested, if one looks at the original or even the one -- the amended one, of December, 1999, it's all very different because the jurisprudence of this Tribunal changed dramatically as to the amount of detail and the further details that were added as a result of motions and instructions from the Trial Chamber clearly at that stage didn't involve Stojan Zupljanin because he's never appeared but Mr. Ackerman must understand the original -- he keeps on talking about an original indictment against Brdjanin alone, there never was such a thing. There was always a joint indictment against all three men. As to the military component, I don't know how often we have to keep saying this. There is and always will be a military component to the evidence in this case. This case against Mr. Brdjanin is that he, Talic, Zupljanin and others, were engaged in a criminal joint enterprise which had a number of different components, the police, the army, and the political. And our understanding of the law is that if there is such an enterprise, the actions and the words of persons in furtherance of that joint enterprise are admissible evidence and, again, to assert that Mr. Brdjanin had no control over the military and the like, all of that is a matter of evidence. What we are dealing with here at the moment is the law on what is permissible charging language in an indictment, and we would be criticised if we did not make it clear that we were saying that this was a criminal joint enterprise and that evidence will be led even now as to the military actions that were taken in the course of this joint enterprise in 1992 in the area known as the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I respond very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume Ms. Korner is correct that there was an original indictment charging all three of the people in this case but it's never been served on anyone. I have never seen it. I doubt Your Honours have ever seen it. It apparently rests somewhere in the registry. What I was talking about in regard to the original indictment was the original indictment filed among the pleadings in this case and that original indictment filed among the pleadings in this case charged only Radoslav Brdjanin, did not include all of this language that you see in the current indictment regarding Momir Talic. The second thing is with regard to this issue of joint criminal enterprise. And it seems to me that in the interest of timing, that it might make sense, and I'm just raising this so that Your Honours can begin to think about it and maybe you would prefer that I raise it formally by motion, but it seems to me that it would make sense if the Prosecution contends that there was a joint criminal enterprise, of which Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Talic were a part, that the Chamber should first require the Prosecution to establish to the Chamber's satisfaction, prima facially, that there was such a joint criminal enterprise and that Brdjanin and Talic and anybody else they contend were members of it, because if the Court would find that the Prosecution has failed to establish that prima facially then we could save an enormous amount of time in this case because we are hearing all of these crime-base witnesses on the basis that at some point it will be established that there was a joint criminal enterprise and if it never happens then we've wasted an enormous amount of time. So that might be a solution to the time problem that I know Your Honours perceive with regard to the continuation of this case, if the Prosecution would simply be instructed to order their proof in that way. It might save a great deal of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You want to file a motion, you're of course free to do so. So that was the submission on para 13 -- para 12. Para 13 is very much the same. If I read well the request of the Defence, it amounts to or it's tantamount to the removal or the deletion from that paragraph of any reference to General Talic being commander of the 1st Krajina Corps and member of the ARK Crisis Staff, being responsible for the implementation of the policy of incorporating the ARK into a Serb state. Do you sustain this -- just say "yes" or "no" because obviously the reasoning if you say no, the reasoning is the same I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I sustain my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I don't think you need to respond, Ms. Korner, because -- para 15, that's no problem. Both of you asked for the deletion of that paragraph and that paragraph has indeed been deleted. Para 19, now, this paragraph, in the fourth amended indictment, of December, reads, "General Momir was the commander of the JNA 5th Corps from 19 March, 1992 and on its transition to the 1st Krajina Corps from 19th May, 1992, each of the five corps within the VRS had a corps commander and a command staff all of which were subordinated to General Mladic and the main staff of the VRS." You want this to be -- you want the deletion of reference to General Talic being the commander of the JNA 5th Corps and on it's transition to the first Krajina Corps and that the corps commander and command staff were subordinated to General Mladic and the main staff of the VRS. Do you sustain it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour and this is a little different in that these paragraphs are specifically allegations against General Talic and if these are appropriately in the indictment then it seems that also appropriately in the indictments would be specific allegations against Mr. Zupljanin and maybe other members of the Crisis Staff but this clearly is material that was put in the indictment because General Talic was a co-defendant in the case and for no other reason. It wouldn't have been there had he not been arrested and it should not be there now that he's no longer in the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's in fact background and explanation. That's the trouble with the forms of the indictment here in my view. One is required to set out a full explanation of the events which lead to the specific charges, unlike, I imagine, Your Honour's jurisdiction and mine where you simply have a straight forward allegation. But these are all background paragraphs and they are there to explain how we put the case on -- against accused in relation to each component of it. And clearly, it is important for the Court to know that there was a transformation into the Bosnian Serb Army around the 12th of May and Talic's position therein. But it's one of the things I've always wondered about, whether, when it came to establishing the case one was obliged to establish the background facts as well, but that is background information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Basically, as you know, Mr. Ackerman, the Prosecution seeks to retain this paragraph as it is only removing the bold character from where -- for Talic's name. Same request is directed by the Defence against para 20, in so far as this paragraph contains the duties and lists the duties and responsibilities of General Talic in his capacity as commander. Do you want to sustain and of course the answer is yes, because.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because this follows the previous one. And I suppose you're reply is the same?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And then it's 21. Now, here, this is perhaps a little bit more fundamental because it's not just the description -- background description, of events, but there is also a -- quite a straightforward allegation here. This paragraph, the Defence seeks to delete in so far as it contains references to Talic as a co-perpetrator in the joint criminal enterprise and that his participation in the execution of the common purpose of the enterprise included activities of the Crisis Staff. There is also a reference to Talic allegedly being individually responsible for the conduct of other participants in the joint criminal enterprise, including members of the ARK crisis and those implementing its decision. What's your position in this -- on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's quite substantially altered. If you look at paragraph 20.1 which I think is what you're reading it's quite substantially altered from the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were reading out the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes exactly. I'm just pointing out now before you answer that the amendments that have been applied by the Prosecution are three. Number 1, the name of Talic remains there and some places but it no longer appears in bold. Number 2, the words, "General Momir Talic and others" have -- in other words, five lines from the top of that paragraph, reading, "General Talic and others, and other members of the crisis -- were co-perpetrators in this criminal enterprise and as such, their participation up to Crisis Staff." "General Momir Talic and other," those words are deleted. "General Momir Talic and others," those words are deleted. I suggest Mr. Ackerman reads the proposed amended version. Can you live with that as contrasted with or as compared with the fourth amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm basically satisfied with one exception. The first sentence, if the first sentence were removed, then it would begin with, "The Crisis Staff, later renamed War Presidency was one of the structures," blah blah blah blah blah. There is no justification for singling out General Talic being publicly named as one of the members of the ARK Crisis Staff so if that was just removed and the paragraph read, "The Crisis Staff" and on through what the amendment says, then it would be perfectly acceptable and I think appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I should say one more time, the only legal obligation upon us is to make it absolutely clear in this indictment that General Talic is not charged on this indictment. That's the only obligation we say that we are obliged to follow. And that's why it's been left. We have altered as little as possible because we feel that's the proper thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Paragraphs 21 to 23.1, taken altogether, you notice in the original or in the fourth amended indictment, there is a specific reference to the units which were placed under the command of General Talic. The Defence for Brdjanin wants that to be removed. That is not being accepted by the Prosecution. The only difference between the two versions is that Momir Talic appears in bold in the fourth amended, while it does not appear in bold in the proposed amendments. Is it so fundamentally important for to you have this removed, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it gives the indictment a fundamental military character, which I think it does not deserve. It's my recollection, and Ms. Korner will certainly correct me if I'm wrong but I'm pretty sure I'm right, these paragraphs were added as a result of an objection to the indictment filed by General Talic himself saying that it was not sufficiently specific, the Prosecution resisted that request by General Talic. Judge Hunt ordered that this kind of specificity be put in the indictment. It was done over the Prosecutor's objection and that's how it got there and now the Prosecutor is objecting to it being removed. And it seems to me that it should be removed, that it is pure Talic material, was put there at the request of General Talic and was not part of any of the original indictments in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you want to comment, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm sure that's -- I can't remember exactly but I'm sure that's right. This was the request for further particulars. But again, Your Honour, it's in there because we are going to be leading evidence of what various units did in various areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Para 24, the Defence seeks the deletion in that paragraph of any reference to Talic being the person responsible to carry out a plan to establish and secure a Serb state and to separate the ethnic communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that this included inter alia attacking and destroying non-Serb villages, killing and terrorising the non-Serb population. This is not being -- you're not being met by the Prosecution in this context, Mr. Ackerman, and the only difference between the two texts is the removal of the bold characters. Do you sustain your -- do you retain your position or do you want to change it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I don't change my position, Your Honour. This is a pure allegation against General Talic because he was originally -- he became part of this indictment. It was not there until he became part of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, no comments from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Para 25 and 26 which I suggest we take together, the Defence is seeking the deletion from those two paragraphs of any reference to what Talic's responsibilities and obligations were as a superior for violations of international law of war committed by individuals under his command. Now, this is not being accepted by the Prosecution and when you compare the two texts, the only difference is the bold characters appearing on the -- in the fourth amended indictment are not being retained. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My position is the same as I stated with regard to paragraph 24, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And your position I suppose is the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, may I direct you to paras 27.1 to 27.4, please. The amendments that have been incorporated in the proposed amended indictment are the following. Number 1, the name of General Talic which appeared in bold in the fourth amended indictment no longer appears in bold. Then there are minor grammatical adjustments, namely plural becomes singular, which you don't need to worry about, and then in para 27.2, there is the removal of the words "and military". In other words, the last line of that paragraph, respective positions in the Bosnian Serb political and military power structures it would read now, "Respective position in the Bosnian Serb political structure." In his position, the reference being to Radoslav Brdjanin only and removal of General Talic. What's your position, as far as this proposed amendment is concerned, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour are we speaking 27.1 through 27.4?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The only -- I'm satisfied with the amendment with one exception. In paragraph 27.2, after Radoslav Brdjanin, it seems that it makes sense for Momir Talic's name not to appear so it would say, "Including Radoslav Brdjanin and other members of the ARK Crisis Staff." But it's not a Brdjanin-specific indictment to single out Momir Talic among those members of the Crisis Staff. Otherwise, I'm satisfied with the rest of those paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I will not be asking for your comments unless I see you standing. Thank you. So that is -- then para 32, please, para 33 and para 34. These are simple amendments that, of course, have been necessitated by the severance of Talic, removal of Talic from this case. Each time there is recurrence of the word "each of the accused were" now we have the phrase or the words "the accused was" or "the accused is". I suppose that is -- should not be in any way controversial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not, Your Honour. Those are fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, may I direct you to para 36 now? This is perhaps where you need to both to pay a little bit more attention. Basically, as I read your motion, Mr. Ackerman, more or less you -- with regard to the charges section of the indictment, you are seeking the removal of any reference to Talic, including the following. In para 36, you were seeking for the removal of any indication towards individual and joint responsibility of the accused for the alleged offences. In reality, the proposed amendments are to this effect, name of General Talic is being deleted, and then obviously, wherever you have the recurrence of the words "with each other" that has also been deleted. Are you happy with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I certainly take your word for what has happened. I've not had a chance to read all the way through all of those. If what you say is the case, then, yes, I'm happy. All I ask for was that General Talic's name be removed from those, and that's kind of an obvious request, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the same applies basically, it seems to me, correct me if I am wrong, as far as paras 44, 46, -- 44 and 46. Wherever there was the name of Talic, this has been removed and wherever there was the use of the words "with each other" these also have been removed. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So may I refer you now to para 48, please? And in para 48, you have the deletion of General Talic's name. Otherwise everything remains the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's acceptable, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Paras 50 and 52. Name of Talic has been deleted and there are some consequential grammatical changes, which shouldn't bother you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. It's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The same applies to paras 54 and 56, 58, and 60, and 62, and 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and again I think the amendments are appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I think we have covered all the proposed amendments and when I say proposed, proposed from both sides. And therefore, the matter will be decided later on today by this Chamber in so far as the proposed amendments are concerned. So.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have one query on that. I don't quite understand the procedures on this. If Your Honours order amendments to be made, does that -- I think that doesn't require it to be resigned, it's the same indictment with amendments. That's I think -- but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not sure either, Ms. Korner. In fact it's something that I need to go and discuss with my --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Your Honour gives us the answer we will comply with whatever is required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I can assure of you is it's something that is going to be attended to today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, It's not our idea to sleep on this or to take much time in deciding it. As soon as this sitting is over, in fact we are going to meet to conclude on this and the other. So next point is, in your document, objection to proceeding with the trial under the current indictment, Mr. Ackerman, you are asking for the suspension of evidentiary proceedings or the staying of evidentiary proceedings until this Chamber has approved the new indictment or approved amendments to the indictment. May I have -- may we have your comments on this specific request, Mr. Ackerman? Knowing that we do not intend to proceed with the continuation of hearing of evidence until we decide this, but we are going to decide it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure what Your Honour is asking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. You asked specifically and in a way it is understandable, in another way it may not be so understandable, that this case be stayed as far as the receipt of evidence is concerned, until a new indictment has been filed and approved by the Trial Chamber or a Judge thereof and until the accused has been able to exercise whatever rights the rules of justice and justice may provide him with regard to that new indictment. With this, you have a suggestion or a request that should we decide to amend the indictment, you are expecting that -- or you are pretending a right for your client to have 30 days within which to file pleadings or pleas or whatever. Do you sustain that position? Do you maintain that position? Or do you want to withdraw on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do not withdraw it but I will say this: Until I actually see what the indictment is going to be, it's difficult to tell you my final decision with regard to that. There is not a situation, and the only reason I mentioned 30 days is because that's what the rule says, but there is not a situation where I would require 30 days. There is a situation where I might ask for a few days. One of the -- I think -- largely unresolved issues in this Tribunal is to what extent is surplusage permitted in an indictment and can an indictment be attacked because it contains surplusage and that's based upon the proposition that I set out rather briefly in my motion, and that is that what is relevant evidence, basically as judged by a Trial Chamber based upon what is alleged within the indictment. So the language of the indictment can have large impact upon what the Trial Chamber sees as evidence that's relevant to the case. And if the indictment contains surplus language, the only justification for which would be that it would permit the introduction of evidence that otherwise would not be admissible, then it would seem to me that an arguments could be made that that surplus language should be removed and it seems also to me that that would come under the heading of preliminary motions regarding the indictment as provided for by the rule. I think once I know later today or tomorrow what form the indictment is going to take then I can tell you specifically how I feel about that. But in no event would it be 30 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Assuming just nor argument's sake that you are right, and that there will be a requirement or the need for you to file some kind of response or whatever, would the necessary consequence be for the staying of evidentiary proceedings? Do the -- do you see such a close and intimate nexus between the two such as to make it impossible for this Trial Chamber to proceed with the hearing of evidence without, of course, prejudicing your right, if you have it, to file written pleading arising out of the amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I haven't given than a great deal of thought but I hear very clearly what it is you're saying and I need the Chamber to understand this: If we could go forward with this case tomorrow, I would like to do that, but I don't want to, by doing that, waive a substantive right of Mr. Brdjanin, and I certainly would not intend to waive any substantive right of Mr. Brdjanin. So I'm unsure about how to answer your question. I think, just as a matter of fundamental law, that a trial should not go forward upon an indictment unless it is a final indictment that is legal and appropriate, and if there is pending some attack upon that indictment, then it would seem to me that it's very difficult to go forward even with a waiver. But if Your Honour believes that we can go forward with a waiver by me that would not affect the substantial rights of Mr. Brdjanin, and we could make that pretty air tight on the record, then I wouldn't have any objection because I do feel like this case should go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I put it to you again for argument's sake that whatever amendments are made to the indictment, these are the result or are the consequence of not having General Talic any more a joint accused, a co-accused, in this trial. The end result of any -- of the exercise to amend the indictment can never - it's being suggested to you - bring as a consequence either the aggravation of the situation of your client, as far as charges are concerned, in other words he is not going to be -- to be charged any differently from what he has been charged so far. The charges were and it is being suggested will remain exactly the same as they are until now. And if that is the case, if that is the case, where do you see the prejudice?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, frankly, I don't see any at this point, Your Honour. And that's why I said I really would have no objection going forward as long as it does not involve a waiver of any substantive right of my client and I don't think it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know how many times I have to say the same thing. The amendments, as Your Honour has rightly said, are only those to remove from the indictment a suggestion that General Talic is facing potential conviction on that indictment. It is our submission that Mr. Ackerman has absolutely no right, under the rules, to seek a 30-day adjournment to file pleadings. Rule 50 states, "The Prosecutor may amend an indictment under (A)(i)(C) after the assignment of a case to a Trial Chamber with the leave of that Trial Chamber or a Judge after having heard the parties." And in (A)(2), "After the assignment after case to a Trial Chamber it shall be not necessary -- it shall not be necessary for the amended indictment to be confirmed." Rule (B), Rule 50(B), "If the amended indictment includes new charges, and the accused has already appeared, there is no need -- then there has to be a further appearance," and (C), "The accused shall have a period -- a further period, of 30 days, in which to file preliminary motions pursuant to Rule 72 in respect -- and I emphasise -- of the new charges." So Your Honours, with the greatest respect, Mr. Ackerman does not have a right under the rules on this amendment to file a further objection. Your Honour, my concern is that we have witnesses here. In fact because we thoughts we were sitting in the afternoon, we were expecting to call a witness today but we have four witnesses here and we need to know to be assured that we will shall able to call evidence tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Next point, tell me when we need to stop, Madam Registrar? Okay. Thank you. Now, the decision will be handed down orally by the way and there is no other way of dealing with it without wasting much time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask, will Your Honours then reassemble the Court when you reach the decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will be deciding first on the proposed amendments, secondly whether we are going to stay proceedings, thirdly whether we are giving you or whether you are entitled in case we amend, as we need to amend the indictment in any case, whether you are entitled or whether you will be given any time limit under the rules. Next thing that obviously needs to be addressed, you made a suggestion, or a request, Mr. Ackerman, that now that the two cases are being separated, and that for a good number of months we have been receiving evidence directed against the Brdjanin and Talic as co-accused in this trial, time should be taken to sift from amongst that bulk of evidence, corpus of evidence what is relevant to Brdjanin's case and what is not. This request is being opposed by the Prosecution and may we hear any further submissions in addition to what you have put in writing on this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not very material to me when that process is carried out. It could even be carried out at the close of the Prosecution's case, as far as I'm concerned, but it seems it to me there does come a time when it's important for the Brdjanin Defence to know what case it has to answer. And it's my contention that a great deal of the evidence, not a great deal but at least some portion of the evidence that exists in the record right now would not have been admitted had it not been for the presence of General Talic in the case. And I think at some point the Court must decide what of that evidence becomes part of whatever the indictment will be against Mr. Brdjanin as we continue this case. But I'm not suggesting to you that we need to stop all proceedings and spend the next month going through that process. I think that process can be carried out over the course of this trial without delaying the trial in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Ackerman, you're putting in the same pot two completely different things. One, there is no doubt that the Trial Chamber eventually will have to decide which of those documents are relevant to your client and which may not be relevant at all. But that is a separate exercise which should not be mentioned at this stage because that's our problem and not yours, neither the Prosecution's nor yours. You are mature enough to know or experienced enough to know that the Prosecutor can stand up and say, "Every single document that has been tendered it -- is relevant." At that point in time, what is your request? The Prosecutor tells you, all of them are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's probably the Prosecutor's position that all of them are relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are all experienced here and this is why I'm preempting the issue because I had no doubt that this is what Ms. Korner will have stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question of relevance is always one for the Trial Chamber and it has always been the case since we started this trial that issues of relevance were going to be decided later on in the case. That's what Your Honour said in your preliminary remarks before we started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Many of them are not relevant or not relevant at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that but I'm just saying the question of relevance, I think, has changed as a result of the severance in this case and so a new approach must be taken to that issue and the only way it affects Mr. Brdjanin, Your Honour, is that there must come a time when Mr. Brdjanin is made aware of what case it is he has to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that arise from the documentation or from the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It arises from what the Prosecution has been able to prove from their evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's at the end of the -- of the closing of the case for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely. I think I just said that it a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner do you want to comment on it this? Okay. So that is again another matter that will be decided. I think that covers most of what has come to the surface in the wake of the severance of the two accused. Are there any matters that you would like to raise, keeping in mind that we have ten minutes before we are supposed to break. Otherwise, if any argument that you are bringing up now raising, needs more than ten minutes, we better stop now and resume after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know is the answer, but I have to raise what happened in the Appeals Chamber on Thursday. I'm not sure how long that is going to take. I think it probably may take more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is about the Randal --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is about the Randal affair and what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have not consulted with my colleagues as yet because I didn't have the chance but just to inform you that last Friday, I asked for a copy of the transcript of the proceedings before the Appeals Chamber and I have read them. What I haven't read, because it hasn't been given to me, is a copy of the Boston Globe article which supposedly contains an interview with Mr. Ackerman, but again, I mean, I must make it clear that this is one topic that I have not yet discussed with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well it may be as well Your Honour if we were to break, we can provide Your Honours with a copy of the Boston Globe because it formed part of the appellant's brief. What I am afraid I managed to mislay wholly somehow -- I should have given it to Ms. Gustin straight away but I didn't was Mr. Ackerman's e-mail to solicitors for the appellants and their response which was put in to the trial -- the Appeals Chamber. I was provided with a copy on the morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That I haven't seen either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I'm afraid I may have to ask if perhaps one of your staff could speak to the senior legal officer to the Appeals Chamber and see if he can provide a copy of that. Perhaps -- I wouldn't mind a copy either because I've lost mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically, I mean, I have read -- let me just hear you, Mr. Ackerman, for a couple of minutes, not more, on this. In a way, I understand what your stand is and what your preoccupation or your concern is. I want to make it clear also that I will be suggesting to my colleagues to approach this not from the importance of the appeals hearing or decision, because that is - I consider - to be something which is completely irrelevant to the point that is being raised by you, arising from the interview which Mr. Ackerman gave to the Boston Globe. What's your position, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I can state it very briefly. My original position regarding this matter has changed a little bit but not very much. And I think I have -- it's on the record somewhere in this case that I did change that position, I'll find it if you'd like me it to but in any event, my position is this: Having spoken with the other journalist involved, he was here, he spoke with the Prosecution and he spoke with me, and at that point, my position changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other journalist involved without mentioning a name is the one who is supposed to have been interpreting?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I had originally thought it was a different interpreter and that's when I first learned it was this journalist. At that point it became clear to me that -- and I looked at the article that the second journalist wrote, at that point it became clear to me that the Randal article was largely correct, as far as it went, but it failed to put the whole issue into context and therefore was misleading and that it was necessary to cross-examine Mr. Randal for the purpose of showing the context in which the article was written. I agreed with Mr. Koumjian or I suggested to Mr. Koumjian that I would have no objection to admitting the article written by the other journalist because it did contain reference to the context in which the alleged remarks were made where the Randal article did not. And so if the Prosecution still insists on using the Randal article as opposed to the other one, then I must still insist that he be brought here for cross-examination. Now, somewhere there was confusion generated with regard to that and I think it probably was my fault there was confusion generated with regard to that, I didn't intend for that to happen but I think just now I have stated my position about as clearly as I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, I think there is so much that needs to be said on this position that I think we better do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least I know what the position of Mr. Ackerman is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I was a little bit confused actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think there is anybody who wasn't confused about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I suggest that instead of reassembling in a few minutes to discuss this that you go ahead with the task you have before you and if there is anything further to discuss with regard to the Randal matter we could do that when you announce your decision later today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Your Honour is going to -- sorry I understood we were going to have a break and then come back to discuss the Randal position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. This is was just because I didn't quite know what Mr. Ackerman's position was because one time he seemed to be accepting the article or the correctness of the article. At the same time, still requiring the -- Mr. Randal to be here for cross-examination to rectify the wrong impression that the article may be giving or may have given so that is where I was confused obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Mr. Ackerman -- I think Your Honour has now misunderstood. Mr. Ackerman is suggesting that we don't have break and come back and discuss it. He's suggesting that we don't discuss it until you've reached a decision on the indictment. That's what I was clarifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. We discuss Randal and then we reach -- because the first we have to conference amongst ourselves on the indictment and give instructions for the elaboration of at least a few points that we may require in giving the oral decision. Then we meet here to discuss the Randal -- we may actually decide the issue before we move on to discuss the Randal thing but we may require to postpone giving the oral decision until after the discussion on the Randal but first we have a break and then we will.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the break being -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 30 minutes, I think we need, 30 minutes at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 30 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I take a little time it to run through what is rather a complicated history now because it's important I think for a number of reasons that we sort this. Your Honour, the Appeals Chamber at the end of the hearing on Thursday, as Your Honour knows, because you've read the transcript, Judge Meron asked me or he said this, "The situation before us now in the light of the e-mail which was mentioned is perhaps less than crystal clear. I would be grateful to the Prosecutor to Ms. Korner if she would tell us this. Assume that it is confirmed that Mr. Brdjanin does no longer contest the accuracy of the quotations, would you still need in these circumstances a subpoena?" And my response to that was this: "First, the point that I'm trying to make is that although Mr. Ackerman has sent this extraordinary e-mail not to the court but to the appellant saying he no longer wishes to contest it, that admission has to be made before the Trial Chamber. Then if the Trial Chamber admits the article we certainly, on behalf of the Prosecution don't require Mr. Randal to attend. Mr. Ackerman, however, in order, as I understand it, still to have this article admitted says that we must call, says the Trial Chamber must order the journalist to appear so that he can question him about the context. But at the moment, as I say, all of this is unclear. We do not wish to call Mr. Randal. We took the statement from Mr. Randal to confirm the accuracy of the quotes. If those are no longer disputed, that ends our interest in calling him provided the article is admitted." Now, Your Honour, it arose as Your Honour well remembers in this way, that the article was objected to and a statement had been taken from Mr. Randal, and I think it's worth reminding Your Honours and Mr. Ackerman of what is in the statement as a result of what Mr. Ackerman has been saying since then. It is to this effect, Your Honour, if you would forgive me one moment while I just extract -- it was attached to the -- sorry. Yes. Your Honour, the statement taken from Mr. Randal said this, in respect of the interview. "The other journalist X and I interviewed Brdjanin at the Presidency in Banja Luka. He was open with us and quite happy to talk. X was a former Fulbright scholar in Belgrade and spoke fluent Serbo-Croat. We therefore did not need an outside interpreter." Your Honour, then I have looked at the transcripts in which these matters were discussed before Your Honours because they were supplied to the solicitors for Mr. Randal with the leave of Your Honours. It arose first on January the 21st when I said that the witness declined to attend, and Mr. Ackerman at page 653, stated that he required Mr. Randal to attend because he objected to the use of any newspaper articles to prove a fact at issue in this case and this one falls into the same position and it may very well be that this person doesn't want to come because they can't substantiate what they wrote in the article. The appeals Chamber was then told that apparently Mr. Ackerman hadn't read the article so the matter was adjourned from that day. Then it arose again -- I'm sorry, in the same day, and Your Honour dealt with it, and then again in respect of the witness summons, on the 26th of February, I raised the matter again and asked whether it was required for the journalist to attend because whether there was going to be cross-examination upon the content of the interview, and we asked Mr. Ackerman to reconsider the request that the journalist attend saying that we were content purely to put the article in. And Mr. Ackerman at that stage said to Your Honour, and this is at page 2284 of the transcript, "Ms. Korner has touched the very matter that is the essence of my challenge and that is that the person who could actually understand what Mr. Brdjanin was saying was hostile to Mr. Brdjanin politically, and it's my contention that what was written down was not what Mr. Brdjanin said." I am assuming from that that Mr. Brdjanin had provided instructions that the quotes or -- were inaccurate. Your Honours issued the witness summons and it was referred to on a number of occasions after that but Your Honour the only other point that Mr. Ackerman made about it was this, and this was on the 1st of March at page 2527 of the transcript, he was objecting to the admission on the basis that it was after the period specified in the indictment. And then he broached for the first time that the subject matter of the interview was Mr. Brdjanin as a minister of the government was being asked his views regarding the cantonisation plan put forward by Vance and Owen and he dealt with -- the Vance-Owen Plan and stated that was what he was being asked to comment upon, that is Mr. Brdjanin, his client. And that effectively was the last discussion, save for the question of the witness summons and when it was going to be served up. Your Honour, therefore at no stage and this is the point I was forced to make, although Mr. Ackerman then -- and I think Your Honour now looked at the Boston Globe article, gave an interview to the Boston Globe in which he stated that, having said this, "The Prosecution entered the article to as evidence to show that the accused had the intent to commit the crime of genocide, Brdjanin's lawyer John Ackerman said in an interview. That if Randal's article were to be entered as evidence the Defence should be allowed to cross-examine the reporter. By questioning Randal, Ackerman wanted to bring up the context of the quotation. Specifically, the Defence claims that Brdjanin was answering a question about the Vance-Owen Peace Plan which would have divided Bosnia into cantonments, hence Brdjanin's quoted remarks should be understood as descriptive not prescriptive, according to Ackerman." Your Honour, there was then that correspondence that was sent to the lawyers acting for Mr. Randal. The situation, Your Honour, is this, at the moment, that apparently Mr. Randal -- I'm sorry, Mr. Ackerman on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin no longer contests any of the accuracy of the quotes. The Prosecution therefore would repeat its application for Your Honours to admit that article as evidence and would not therefore propose to call Mr. Randal. What is important, clearly, is that the Appeals Chamber must be informed of what the situation actually is because it makes the whole matter completely moot as it is a lot of expense has been spent on this when it appears it wasn't necessary and great questions of principle are being raised based on a set of facts which may be thoroughly erroneous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It may still be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Your Honours what I'm asking now is that Mr. Ackerman make it clear what his position is now in respect of that article and on what basis therefore the journalist should be required to attend rather than the article being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this morning is a difficult morning. And let me speak of that a bit. First of all, Rule 50 says that an indictment may not be amended until the Chamber or a Judge thereof has heard the parties. I made it clear this morning that I had not seen the proposed amended indictment until 20 minutes or so before I walked into this courtroom. In spite of that, the Chamber decided to go forward on the theory that I could be heard in the context of Your Honours' directing us through the indictment. It may be the case that I have said everything that is important to be said about that but I don't know because I still have not had an opportunity to really go deeply into that indictment. And so just for the record, I want to say that I believe Rule 50(A)(i)(c) has been violated because there has been no meaningful opportunity for me to be heard regarding the Prosecution's proposed amendment. In addition, I had no notice whatsoever that the Randal issue would be brought before the Chamber today. I have none of the documents involved. I have none of the transcripts involved, I have none of the paperwork involved. And so I feel uncomfortable discussing that in any detail at this point. I will say this: Throughout this process, it has been the Prosecution's position that they would rather have before you a misleading account of what happened at that meeting rather than a true account of what happened at that meeting. The article written by the other journalist is a full account setting both the context of that meeting and setting forth what Mr. Brdjanin was asked and what he said. It is the account which gives you the truth of what was going on and with that account, the Prosecution can then not argue that it has anything to do with this case. The only way the Prosecution can argue that it has anything to do with this case is if the Randal article comes in, which is incomplete and does not set the context. So that's the first thing. I have no objection to the article the other journalist wrote coming in because it is complete. And that's the evidence that should be before Your Honours. Now, the second thing. Ms. Korner complains about my e-mail to the lawyers representing Randal. That e-mail was designed to correct what was a misleading impression that was being given to the Appeals Chamber by the Prosecutor, and I thought it was outrageous and inappropriate for the Prosecutor to so mislead the Appeals Chamber and I therefore sent an e-mail to the lawyers for Randal saying the Prosecution's assertion that there is no other source for this evidence is not true. And they are misleading the Appeals Chamber by saying that because I have already told the Prosecutor that I would accept the article written by the other journalist. It is an acceptable source, another source, of that evidence and it's the appropriate source of that evidence. And now for Ms. Korner to come in here today and accuse me of some kind of wrong doing I find outrageous. The wrong doing was on her part for misleading the Trial Chamber to the proposition that there is no other source of this evidence. There is another source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not the Trial Chamber the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Appeals Chamber. And I felt compelled to let the lawyers for Randal know about that. And that that was misleading and that was an untrue statement to the Appeals Chamber. I do not want to discuss it further without consulting the documents and if you want me to discuss it further after having done that, I'm perfectly willing to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not going to respond to the sort of invective that's being used because it's unnecessary. But it is actually a very simple question and I think it is one that needs to be answered straight away before the Appeals Chamber spends any longer on this. Is the accuracy of the quotes that appear in Mr. Randal's article a subject matter of dispute? That's the only question I'm asking, and that, Mr. Ackerman, regardless of anything else, must be able to answer and he appears to have already answered it in the e-mails but it must be put on record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Assuming that stage is reached and surpassed, it seems to me, from what I have read, that in any case, Mr. Ackerman would require the presence of Mr. Randal here for cross-examination. At that point in time, or should that be so, is it your responsibility, is it the Prosecution's responsibility, to procure, assuming that the article itself is first admitted in evidence, would it remain your responsibility to bring forward Mr. Randal to be cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it wouldn't, because as I said, our interest was only that the article was admitted and that the accuracy of the quotes was not in dispute. Thereafter, if Mr. Ackerman wished to secure the attendance of Mr. Randal, it would be a matter for him. We are only required to call evidence -- to call witnesses if we want to put in that witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm trying to make things clear because at that point in time, the conclusion, if what you have just stated is correct, the conclusion would be twofold. Number 1, that the whole process of subpoenaing Mr. Randal for the purposes mentioned or indicated in that subpoena would no longer hold water.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Number 2, there may still be the need for a subpoena to be issued against Mr. Randal if Mr. Randal refuses to turn up to be cross-examined by you on whatever it is you want to cross-examine him upon. And that would potentially bring us back to square one. So Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if we are talking about resources and the efficient and proper use of resources, we should leave the matter as it stands because it makes no sense to restart this whole process and go through all of that all the way up through the Appeals Chamber again because Mr. Randal will again oppose the subpoena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- I think, I don't know, I don't want to overstep in any way, but as I see it, we could be really wishful thinking, doing some wishful thinking that this may be solved in the way that maybe has been understood or has been suggested because in reality, if I read you well, irrespective of the position that you are taking vis-a-vis his article as a stand-alone article or in juxtaposition with the article of the other journalist, as I read you, you still want to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If his article is going to come into evidence, Your Honour, his article is less reliable than a 92 bis statement. I can have those people brought for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But then you're forcing my hand and I will essentially come to the conclusion that I need to give you a time limit within which you have to confirm officially to this Trial Chamber what you may have written in the e-mail, and specifically asking you to declare whether you are accepting on the face of it the correctness of the quotes attributed to your client reserving of course any further right you may have to cross-examine the witness on whatever you would like to cross-examine him on, because that will impact on the possible decision that we may need to take as to whether to allow the document in evidence or not. And also, irrespective of whether there should be the other article that you refer to, of X, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I've said all I can safely say about that right now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ackerman, it is the decision of this Trial Chamber to give you until 11.00 of tomorrow morning to file a declaration specifying whether you still contest the accuracy of the quotes attributed by Mr. Randal in his article to your client, and secondly, should you no longer contest the accuracy of those quotes, whether you require the attendance, the presence, of Mr. Randal here for the purposes of cross-examining him on whatever you think you may need to cross-examine him upon. And following that, we will communicate the -- your statement then to the Appeals Chamber. We are not going to -- I'm not going to entertain any further arguments on respective accusations of misleading, et cetera, so that is being left apart. Now, I have missed -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Would you like to raise any further matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, a couple, if I may, the first is this. Mr. Ackerman was -- e-mails are the topic of the moment, sent an e-mail by us to the United States last week requesting an answer about two of the Rule 92 bis witnesses that he had not objected to but that objection had been made on behalf of General Talic. That is 7.191 and 7.192. And again, Your Honours, because we are trying to organise witnesses, Your Honours ordered that each appear for cross-examination, limited to one hour, but there was, as I understood it, no objection on behalf of Brdjanin to these witnesses so we would like to confirm that that still stands, and that they can be entered under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know why this is being brought to your attention, I discussed it with Ms. Korner and Ms. Gustin this morning and I told them that I had left these in Texas and that if they would tell me I would look at them and let them know today what my position was. I don't know why it has to be brought to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I take it you'll be acting on this and that you will be cooperating with him again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, then, this, Your Honour promised, said that you would let us know about this November -- these November dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I have not discussed that with my colleagues as yet. I promise you we'll come back to you on this later on this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me just make sure that I make it clear that I would object strongly to any change being made in the schedule. I have matters scheduled in the United States, including some medical matters, during that time, and I see no reason for changing it. I think we are shortening up the trial a great deal with the severance and I don't think that we need to recover time, and I would strongly urge that the schedule as published be followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's entirely a matter for Your Honours but I would say this. The idea of co-counsel is that one counsel has to be absent, the other counsel can take over and indeed Your Honour has confirmed with Mr. Ackerman and I think it was Mr. Zecevic at the time, that if they had been to be absent someone else could take over. That's all I want to say on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there is this -- I just have to say this. There is this proposition that has been asserted a few times by the Prosecutor that the idea of co-counsel is that there will be somebody to take over if one or the other can't be here. If you look at the directive of assignment on counsel, the idea of co-counsel is to be provided in a case that is sufficiently complicated that it requires two attorneys to handle it. The directive assumes that co-counsel will not be provided in every case but only in those cases that are sufficiently complicated to require two lawyers to handle it and it never in the directive or in any other writings that have come from the registry or the Tribunal, as far as I know, has it been seen as a tag-team situation with co-counsel -- if one is absent, the other can be present. That can happen on occasion, there is no question about it, but that's not what the idea was. That's not why it was instituted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a matter for Your Honours I just wanted to know so we can organise witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally, Your Honours, it's this, it's along the same lines of what Mr. Ackerman has just been saying. Is it Your Honours' intention to limit the time in which the Prosecution will be allowed to present its case? Because that is something we must know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe again that is something that I have on my agenda to discuss with the other two judges. And it in addition to what you have just stated, we may have news to communicate to you later on with regard to Prijedor, giving that substantial amount of evidence is -- has been and still being given in the Stakic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's finished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's finished?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Stakic closed its case last Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we need to discuss amongst ourselves first and then we will -- we may eventually come to the conclusion of limiting your time. However, before this is the last point that I had on my agenda gentleman which I was going to refer you to. When we last met it was understandable and we wouldn't have considered it to be otherwise possible, to have some time during which you would reorganise sort of your case now that General Talic is no longer in it. And this last week was supposed to serve precisely that purpose.
