It didn't -- we didn't mean to say, and I suppose you didn't mean to take it that this week would be sufficient, would be enough, but it would be the beginning of a process, an ongoing process, which you would undertake to realign the whole strategy, number of witnesses, et cetera. I think you now owe us some kind of an indication as to whether the exercise -- this exercise that you should have started during the past week is indicative of any substantive or substantial change in the expectations or forecasts of this Tribunal with regard to the duration and progress of this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as Your Honour rightfully said, we spent a goodly proportion of last week when we weren't or when I wasn't in the Appeals Chamber, considering how to present this case. We have reached certain preliminary conclusions, particularly in respect of whether we now proceed to call evidence in relation to all the municipalities. We have already I think told Your Honours and the Defence that we were reducing the amount of evidence for certain municipalities that would be reduced to one or two witnesses. But it's I'm afraid a bit of a chicken and an egg situation. In other words we need to know for sure whether we are going to be told your case must end by a certain date because in each case, the difficulty is that there is cogent evidence, we would submit, because we have reached certain preliminary conclusions and we hope it to finalise them today, after Your Honours have sat. Can I just say this about Prijedor, though? The whole way it's developed is highly unfortunate that these witnesses have been testifying, some of them for the second or third time in Stakic. But it is we would submit really one of the most important municipalities that Your Honours are going to hear about. We would say that if anything is genocide, what happened in Prijedor was genocide. And we have the same problem as to how we are going to deal with this as indeed, and I accept entirely, does Mr. Ackerman, who has to look through transcripts of all these witnesses' testimony. But I don't know what Your Honours have in mind on that but we would submit that we should be permitted to call the evidence that we've listed. It's a culling already of a great deal of evidence, but it really is an important municipality. As to any other aspects of this case, it will make a difference, it's rather more difficult to formulate the precise method of doing it without longer time which I'm not asking for any time off, we will deal with it in the periods when we are not in court, exactly to what extent we need the military evidence in the same fullness that we would have certainly called it were General Talic an accused in this trial. For example, I can say straight away it's highly unlikely that the expert military witness who is listed will be called. But for the moment, all we can do is say that certainly Kljuc will proceed as anticipated and we would wish to proceed with Prijedor in the same way. But Your Honour, anything else, I think really, we have to know whether we are going to be given, as it were, a time limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me just -- I think I've said it before but I want to say it again. Prijedor is a potential nightmare for us in the sense of the enormous amount of material that's available for each of the witnesses, the Prosecutor intends to call. And I haven't yet figured out how we are going to get through that material and be prepared to cross-examine those witnesses at the time they come. It may very well be that that schedule break that we have in November would be a good time to get through a large portion of that material, at least. It certainly can't be done while I am busy preparing for each witness as we go on with the trial. But it's a monumental undertaking and when Your Honours see the amount of testimony that has already been taken from some of these witnesses, you will understand what I'm talking about. And I couldn't possibly ethically not go through that material before I cross-examine any of these witnesses so I don't know how we are going to work that out but it's something that I need to you understand is a big problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How many witnesses of Prijedor, I mean, in addition to the witnesses that have given evidence or let's -- let me phrase it in a different manner. Do you intend to bring forward all the witnesses that have given evidence in Stakic? Or some of them?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, some. There is a list that's already been prepared, I'm not sure we've handed it in. There are I think only about off the top of my head, three or four witness who have never testified before. Every other witness has testified in at least one trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So there is a number of witnesses that have testified in Stakic who you want to bring over.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To testify here. There is a number, a small number of witnesses, that haven't testified in Stakic that you would like to produce.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But have testified in one of the other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, Your Honour, I think there are literally only about three or four that have not testified before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there anyway we could proceed by applying any of the existing provisions in the rules of guaranteeing in any case and in each case a cross-examination to the Defence while doing away with the need of bringing forward the witness to testify in chief? In other words --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Put the transcripts in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that would be perfectly possible. It's one of the solutions we were thinking of, if that was acceptable, the transcript would go in with any -- some of the witnesses will give additional evidence which was not adduced in the Stakic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With the understanding that should there be anything in the transcripts, in the Stakic or in any other case, any reference to Mr. Brdjanin, that is redacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the witnesses would have to give that evidence orally before Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. If we could live with that, we would definitely be prepared to give a limited time within which, because obviously the Defence will have to go through the documentation, would still spare us and save us a lot of time in examination-in-chief, if that is something that you could agree upon. Something that we are obviously going to think about, and this is what I meant when I said I need to discuss -- this is an item that I have on the agenda for discussion with my two colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the other method of course is for Your Honours to take note within the trial of adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that is another option that we have. This is why, if you refer to what I said a minute ago, to the various options that are provided under the rules. That is another option.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, so far Rule 94 really hasn't been used at all but it seems to me as I think we said a long time ago, for example, in respects of Keraterm, I think all the other cases, save for Tadic that come from this area are still awaiting appeal. But in the case of Keraterm there was a plea, and if it could be -- if Your Honours were to take note and the Defence didn't wish to challenge the facts that are were -- the agreed facts of that plea, that would save obviously having to call any witnesses at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed facts in a plea, I wouldn't -- I would rather be cautious about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, but it was incorporated into the judgement, so it's adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is an adjudicated fact because the two parties agreed upon them. But as far as Brdjanin is concerned, that would be what in Latin my ancestors would say, res inter alios acta something that has been agreed upon by others with whom he has got no association. Yes, you have, because you were a party, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, can I just say this? Taking Mr. Ackerman's point, if the answer is that he won't -- we anticipate starting Prijedor at the end of this month, give or take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would expect you to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Therefore, we haven't yet notified any of the witnesses when they are required to attend it. At least I don't think we have but if Mr. Ackerman is saying that he wants to break in November to look at all of that, and wants us not to call any evidence on Prijedor, then we will have to skip Prijedor again and move on to one of the other municipalities we know definitely we will still be calling evidence on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That could also be another alternative.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But again we need to have that very effectively we need to know by tomorrow if Mr. Ackerman is going to say because of the huge amount of documentation, I won't be in a position to deal with it until after the November break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By tomorrow, Mr. Ackerman has still got to read the Randal papers, which I hope he has here in The Hague and not left back in Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They are here, Your Honour, and I certainly will have that done by 11.00 tomorrow. With regard to this Prijedor issue, just off the top of my head, I see absolutely no reason that I would oppose the transcripts as you have redacted, as you've suggested, coming in as the Prosecution's direct evidence with whatever additions Ms. Korner needs to make. In other words we don't have to repeat what's already been said in Stakic to Your Honours just to take up time. As long as I have a full opportunity to cross-examine. With regard to getting through the material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Ackerman, I know I'm doing something a little bit abrupt but I would like to stop you here and add something. We all know that there may also be in those transcripts, in that evidence, evidence directed against Stakic which may not be exactly desirable to retain, because it may shed -- it may create an environment, an impression, that may not be helpful to Mr. Brdjanin unless it is relevant to Mr. Brdjanin, okay? So that is also something that you may meet together upon and if there is agreement, I'm sure there will be reference specific reference to Mr. Stakic that we don't need to have in the transcripts. And there may be references to Mr. Stakic that we may need to retain in the transcript. So this is, again, another piece in the exercise that I would like you to undertake together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can tell Your Honour that I have already started the process of going through that material. I'm basically finished with one of the witnesses already. But what I now realise if we are going to do that, that I need to do, is go back through that process again and just note those parts that you just talked about that are totally irrelevant to the Brdjanin case and probably should be redacted along with any reference to Brdjanin. Chances are we can get through that. I think we could probably do that quicker than we could actually bring the witnesses here and have them sit here for two or three days while the direct is repeated. I think it's a good idea and I think we can probably pull it off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely, definitely. So we will be meeting in the course of this week to decide on this -- these issues. It would be very helpful to us if you could also meet in the meantime and at least agree -- stick to Prijedor for the time being -- agree on principle, in principle, that we could adopt this procedure, in other words having the transcript, the evidence given by these witnesses in other cases admitted with redactions as the examination-in-chief, meaning also that you still have a right to put some additional questions should that be necessary, should you feel the need for those, and of course, reserving the cross-examination for the Defence in each and every case, unless that is waived because I may also figure that there may be some instances where cross-examination is not needed. Maybe, I don't know, but I mean that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we will be putting in, in any event, we haven't yet served the motion with the Prijedor Rule 92 witnesses. In fact the whole thing may become a slightly mixed exercise because it's the same thing for most of them. It will be transcripts that we want to enter into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There may be a problem should this arise. I would imagine that some of these witnesses gave evidence in closed session in Stakic and in others?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, no, anything I'm sorry, for the witnesses we have intended to call we have orders from Stakic for disclosure. We've dealt with that, sorry. We've dealt with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When we knew that we were going to use it, with one exception I think there is still one outstanding we need to go back to Judge Schomburg about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm asking you because in my mind I had that impression but I wanted confirmation of it. Witnesses giving evidence in other cases, is it the same or do you require --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Any -- no, Your Honour we have obtained from all other Trial Chambers where these witnesses testified even the non-existent Tadic one for which we had to apply to Judge Jorda the orders for disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So if -- I suggest you try and meet as early as you can, without any involvement of the Trial Chamber or its staff for the time being, then if you reach some kind of agreement, may I kindly ask you to incorporate it into -- in a joint memo to the Trial Chamber, and if there are points on which there is disagreement, then please indicate those as well in the memo to the Trial Chamber so that if necessary, we will reconvene -- we will either discuss them in -- during a normal session or we will reconvene another short Status Conference and discuss them in the Status Conference?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, can I just ask one last question? I think I've had it confirmed but we have had so many different times of sitting and days of sitting it is not possible, as I understand to find a court to sit this Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Apart from the fact I wouldn't like to go public in this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you are public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But can we go into closed session for one minute or private session for one minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we would very much appreciate if you could find some time and meet on this, come back to us with points of convergence and points of divergence. If necessary, we will intervene to make you get nearer to one another on this, Prijedor in particular, because I am sure that we will economise on the Tribunal's resources and on time considerably if we resort to this procedure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my guess is that once we break, I can walk over to Ms. Korner's table over there and we will agree on that procedure. The thing that will cause trouble, and that the Chamber will no doubt have to become involved in, is the redactions because we probably won't agree on all of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we can start with the first witness, Mr. Ackerman, that is an ongoing process. That is an ongoing process. I mean, we would be in a position to contribute there as well because although the whole idea is not to stop, bring in the bulk of this evidence and go through it as a first exercise, we will do that as we go along, witness by witness. The important is perhaps the first witness, what is important. I mean, provided we have sufficient time limit or day or two to go through that evidence, and whatever needs to be redacted, if there is no agreement amongst you, will be redacted by the Trial Chamber taking the safest of -- obviously trying to be -- but without prejudicing the rights and the interests of the Prosecution. May I point out that any cooperation between -- forthcoming from the Defence in this context will not be forgotten. It will be remembered as cooperation. So now before bringing the Status Conference to an end, are there any further points that you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, and as I understand it Your Honours are going to let us know when you're ready to give a judgement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Mr. Ackerman, I suppose that I will ask you the question, are you aware of any complaints that your client might have regarding his state of health or condition of detention?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any. You can ask him if he has any. I don't think he does but he is certainly free to state them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I won't ask you if you are happy but I will just ask you whether you have complaints, any remarks or complaints related to your state of health or the conditions in which you are being kept, detained, at the detention unit. THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Just now, I have none, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the Court now stands adjourned. This Status Conference is over. And we are immediately reconvening as a Trial Chamber and I am going to proceed with the oral decision that I promised you. We are not in closed session. We are in open session. We are going to proceed now with your oral decision. I've got some points here from which I dictated to my legal assistant earlier on. It's not to be taken as a written decision. It's an oral decision. So, this Trial Chamber is seized of Prosecution's request for leave to amend the indictment. This specific request was filed on the 3rd of October and we are also seized of an objection raised by Radoslav Brdjanin, the accused in this trial, an objection to proceeding with this trial under the current indictment. Needless to say, the two requests converge on an essential element, namely whether the current indictment should be amended or not. Before proceeding any further, I would also like to add that we have read and considered the Prosecution's response to the objection of Radoslav Brdjanin to which I have just referred. In our considered opinion, the points that need to be addressed and decided are the following. Number 1, whether any or all of the suggested amendments to the fourth amended indictment ought to be accepted or not, approved or not. The Trial Chamber has heard submissions in this regard during the Status Conference of today and comes to the following conclusion. May I also points out that when I say suggested amendments, I am referring to both your suggested amendments and those which are being suggested by the Defence. As a result of the decision of this Trial Chamber to sever the trial of Radoslav Brdjanin from that of General Momir Talic, the need has undoubtedly arisen to amend the current indictment. Amend it in such a way as to exclude from it any specific indication that could lead to understand that General Talic continues to be charged under it. The Trial Chamber, however, sees no validity in the submission of the Defence for Brdjanin that the removal of any mention of General Talic from the indictment necessarily leads to the consequence or has as a consequence the need to have deleted from the indictment also all references to him, his alleged membership in the ARK Crisis Staff, his command position in the military, and indeed, as has been suggested earlier on today during the Status Conference, the military component of the indictment itself. There is no validity in our considered opinion, in the argument that as a result of General Talic's removal from this case, the substance of the accusations, the charges, brought against Brdjanin ought or need to be impacted. The essence of the indictment is that there was a joint criminal enterprise involving the political, the military and the police sectors, in which Brdjanin was involved and this cannot be changed. Arguing that singling out General Talic should not be allowed now that he is no longer a co-accused in this case is not, on its own standing, a valid argument and can only serve as a basis for having possibly inserted in the indictments or in parts of it additional names, particularly of other persons, allegedly involved in the joint criminal enterprise, but this is not what is being sought and at the present moment or what this Trial Chamber is being asked to do. The first decision that this Trial Chamber therefore comes to is to accept and approve the proposed amendments to the fourth amended indictment, namely those proposed by the Prosecution in its request for leave to amend the indictment, to which I referred to earlier. This is being done by this Trial Chamber pursuant to Rule 50(A)(i)(c). The Trial Chamber does not see that it would be fit and proper to include in the indictment any further amendments, namely any of the amendments that have been suggested by the Defence for Radoslav Brdjanin, except in so far as these may converge with the amendments that are being approved. Secondly, in terms of Brdjanin's objection to proceeding with the trial under the current indictment, the Trial Chamber is being asked to confirm that following the amendments to the indictment, he is entitled to a time limit in which to file preliminary motions or pleas pursuant to Rule 72 as provided in Rule 50(C). Brdjanin claims that he should be given this right even if the amended indictment does not contain new charges or any new charges. He contends that this would still be required and he would be entitled to it in the interests of justice. The Trial Chamber has no option but to reject this request. First, because such time limit is allowed by the rules and applicable only if and when new charges are introduced in the indictment, which we see, we understand, is not the present case. Secondly, because we as a Trial Chamber fail to see how the interests of justice can be better served if such an opportunity is given to the accused Brdjanin in the present circumstances. The Trial Chamber has no doubt at all that the charges brought against Brdjanin remain essentially what they have always been since the fourth amended indictment was approved in December of last year. The accused Brdjanin has also asked that the parties be invited to make submissions on which evidence from the Brdjanin-Talic case is relevant to his case and should be incorporated now in the records of his case for the purpose of proceeding with his -- forward with his trial. The Trial Chamber sees no point in extending any such invitation to the parties, who are free to come to any agreement on this matter amongst themselves if they want to or if they feel the need for it. The Trial Chamber does not at this point see the need to give any directions to either of the parties in this context. The last request of the accused Brdjanin is that the case be stayed as far as the receipt of evidence is concerned until a new indictment has been filed and approved by the Trial Chamber or a Judge thereof, and until accused Brdjanin has been able to exercise whatever rights the rules and justice may provide him with regard to the new indictment. The Trial Chamber has no option but to reject this request, which in part is based on the fact of the prior filing of a new indictment. This now, on the basis of this decision, is no longer a problem. And in part, on unspecified possible rights which, as things are, rebus sic stantibus cannot serve as a basis for such a request. We therefore provide as follows: Pursuant to Rule 50(A)(i)(c) and Rule 54 of the rules, we grant the Prosecution's request for leave to amend the indictment as per the details incorporated in the same document mentioned before. We instruct the Prosecution to file a newly signed, amended version of the indictment as approved by this decision by not later than 2 p.m. of today. You have it already?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is as you state.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think Your Honour is perhaps -- a lot of these witnesses actually want to tell the Court what happened because they fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I won't stop him. I won't stop him. It's just if the need arises.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If the need arises. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure I wouldn't have any objection to an agreement to save him having to go through some these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, of course. You have a right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I did want to ask, do you intend to follow up the decision on the indictment with a written decision or will your oral decision be your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. If you ask for it we may entertain the idea but I think the whole idea it was give an oral decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not asking for it. I'm just asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not bound actually to follow up always with a written decision. I mean the whole idea is to spare, economise on our resources as much as we can and move ahead. It doesn't mean to say that if you would like to ask for certification you're not being given the opportunity. I mean obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just was inquiring because of the language of Rule 73 as to whether or not there would be a follow-up decision written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So shall we leave it at that and adjourn? I thank you for all your contributions and cooperation this morning, without which we would have certainly got stuck, and we will resume tomorrow morning with our labours. I thank you.
